content: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a major cause of hospitalization and mortality in young children. Positioning and mechanical ventilation are commonly employed to alleviate respiratory distress and enhance oxygenation in hospitalized patients. However, prone positioning (lying on the abdomen) has been associated with sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) in infants under six months of age, leading to recommendations that young infants be placed on their back (supine). Despite this, prone positioning may serve as a non-invasive method to improve oxygenation in individuals with ARDS and may provide a survival benefit in those requiring mechanical ventilation. It is important to note that there are significant differences in respiratory mechanics between adults and infants. While the respiratory system undergoes substantial development during the first two years of life, the physiological differences in airway function between adults and children diminish by the age of six to eight years. Additionally, the risk of SIDS is reduced in hospitalized infants undergoing artificial ventilation. Therefore, an updated review focusing on positioning strategies for infants and young children with ARDS is necessary. This review updates prior versions published in 2005, 2009, and 2012. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of different body positions in hospitalized infants and children aged four weeks to 16 years with ARDS. The search for relevant studies included CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL databases, covering the period from January 2004 to July 2021. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared two or more body positions for managing ARDS in hospitalized infants and children. Six trials were included in the review, comprising four cross-over trials and two parallel randomized trials, with a total of 198 participants aged between four weeks and 16 years. Of these, all but 15 participants were mechanically ventilated. Four trials compared prone and supine positions. One trial compared the prone position to good-lung dependent positioning (where the patient lies on the side of the healthier lung) and good-lung independent positioning (where the patient lies on the side opposite the healthier lung). Another trial compared good-lung dependent and good-lung independent positions. When prone and supine positions were compared in mechanically ventilated patients, no data were available on episodes of apnea or mortality due to respiratory events. There were no conclusive findings regarding oxygen saturation (SaO2), blood gases (PCO2 or PO2), or lung function (PaO2/FiO2 ratio). However, prone positioning was associated with an improvement in the oxygenation index (FiO2% × MPAW/PaO2) in both parallel trials and one cross-over study. Derived indices of respiratory mechanics, such as tidal volume, respiratory rate, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), were also reported. A parallel study found a decrease in tidal volume in the prone group compared to the supine group. However, a cross-over study found no conclusive results for respiratory compliance, changes in PEEP, or airway resistance when comparing prone and supine positions. One study reported adverse events, but there were no conclusive findings regarding potential harm between groups in terms of extubation, endotracheal tube obstruction, pressure ulcers, or hypercapnia (elevated arterial carbon dioxide levels). Another study compared supine positioning to good-lung dependent and independent positions. There was no conclusive evidence of differences in PaO2 between supine and good-lung dependent positioning, supine and good-lung independent positioning, or good-lung dependent and independent positioning. The included studies did not consistently address potential biases, making the risk of bias in the findings unclear. Although the evidence suggests that prone positioning may offer some advantages, there is insufficient evidence to make definitive recommendations. The evidence supporting the benefit of positioning to improve oxygenation in mechanically ventilated children with ARDS is of low certainty. Given the increased risk of SIDS associated with prone positioning and the potential for lung injury with artificial ventilation, it is recommended that hospitalized infants and children be placed in the prone position only under continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
